claim: PRC2 is a key chromatin modifier responsible for methylation of lysine 27 in histone H3.
source: Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) is a key chromatin modifier responsible for methylation of lysine 27 in histone H3.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PRC2 function, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: PRC2 has been shown to interact with thousands of RNA species in vivo.
source: PRC2 has been shown to interact with thousands of RNA species in vivo, but understanding the physiological function of RNA binding has been hampered by the lack of separation-of-function mutants.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Preferential binding of G-quadruplex RNA by PRC2 is conserved between Homo sapiens and Chaetomium thermophilum.
source: Preferential binding of G-quadruplex RNA is conserved, surprisingly using different protein elements.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Key RNA-binding residues in PRC2 are spread out along the surface of EZH2.
source: Key RNA-binding residues are spread out along the surface of EZH2, with other subunits including EED also contributing, and missense mutations of some of these residues have been found in cancer patients.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and HDX-MS data presented in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Missense mutations of some RNA-binding residues in EZH2 have been found in cancer patients.
source: Key RNA-binding residues are spread out along the surface of EZH2, with other subunits including EED also contributing, and missense mutations of some of these residues have been found in cancer patients.
evidence: This is supported by reference to cancer patient data from a database.

claim: PRC2 specifically catalyzes mono-, di- and tri-methylation of lysine 27 on histone H3 (H3 K27).
source: PRC2 specifically catalyzes mono-, di- and tri-methylation of lysine 27 on histone H3 (H3 K27), which is a hallmark for repressed chromatin and provides a chromatin structure that is repressive to transcription (Cao et al., 2002; Czermin et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2002; Yuan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: H3K27 methylation is a hallmark for repressed chromatin.
source: PRC2 specifically catalyzes mono-, di- and tri-methylation of lysine 27 on histone H3 (H3 K27), which is a hallmark for repressed chromatin and provides a chromatin structure that is repressive to transcription (Cao et al., 2002; Czermin et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2002; Yuan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The PRC2 core complex contains four subunits: EZH2 (or EZH1), SUZ12, EED, and RBBP4.
source: The PRC2 core complex contains four subunits: (1) EZH2 (enhancer of zeste homolog 2) or its closely related homolog EZH1, (2) SUZ12 (suppressor of zeste 12), (3) EED (embryonic ectoderm development) and (4) RBBP4 (retinoblastoma binding protein 4) (Margueron and Reinberg, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PRC2 composition supported by citation.

claim: EZH2 contains the enzymatic SET domain which catalyzes the transfer of methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to H3 K27.
source: EZH2 contains the enzymatic SET (Su[var]3–9, enhancer of zeste, trithorax) domain, which catalyzes the transfer of methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to H3 K27 (Rea et al., 2000; Dillon et al., 2005; Joshi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PRC2 binds RNA promiscuously in vitro and in vivo.
source: PRC2 binds RNA promiscuously in vitro and in vivo (Davidovich et al., 2013, 2015), meaning that it binds many natural RNAs with affinities within the same order of magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: PRC2's promiscuous RNA binding can be explained by PRC2 recognizing short tracts of G's and G-quadruplexes.
source: This promiscuous binding can be explained by PRC2 recognizing short tracts of G's and G-quadruplexes, small motifs which are ubiquitous in the transcriptome (Wang et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: An unstructured region (residues 342–368) of mouse EZH2 that has been proposed to bind RNA is not phylogenetically conserved.
source: An unstructured region (residues 342–368) of mouse EZH2 that has been proposed to bind RNA (Kaneko et al., 2010) is not phylogenetically conserved (Jiao and Liu, 2015), and more important elements for RNA interaction are now apparent (see below).
evidence: This is supported by prior research and findings in this study.

claim: ctPRC2 has specificity for poly(G) RNA.
source: ctPRC2 had specificity for poly (G) RNA, while having the lowest affinity for poly (A) RNA (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ctPRC2 has the lowest affinity for poly(A) RNA.
source: ctPRC2 had specificity for poly (G) RNA, while having the lowest affinity for poly (A) RNA (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ctPRC2 preferred binding to RNA sequences capable of folding into G-quadruplexes.
source: Second, ctPRC2 preferred binding to RNA sequences capable of folding into G-quadruplexes ((GGAA)10, (G4A4)4 and G40) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: ctPRC2 has strong preference for (GGAA)10 over (GA)20 RNA despite having the same nucleotide composition.
source: For example, (GGAA)10 and (GA)20 RNA have the same nucleotide composition, but ctPRC2 has strong preference for (GGAA)10, which is capable of forming G-quadruplexes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The affinity of ctPRC2 for G-quadruplex-forming RNAs is cation-specific.
source: Third, the affinity for G-quadruplex-forming RNAs was cation-specific, as illustrated by the fold change of Kdapp in K+ buffer versus Li+ buffer (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: K+ stimulates G-quadruplex conformation while Li+ does not.
source: K+ stimulates G-quadruplex conformation while Li+ does not, so the fold change larger than one indicates a specific interaction between ctPRC2 and the folded G-quadruplex conformation of (GGAA)10, (G4A4)4 and G40 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cation effects on G-quadruplex structures.

claim: The cation specificity for binding to G-quadruplex RNAs shows the same trend for ctPRC2 and hsPRC2.
source: The cation specificity for binding to the G-quadruplex RNAs and lack of cation specificity for binding to other RNAs remarkably shows the same trend for ctPRC2 and hsPRC2 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The regulatory moiety of ctPRC2 has RNA-binding affinity comparable to the entire ctPRC2 complex.
source: Interestingly, the regulatory moiety had RNA-binding affinity comparable to the entire ctPRC2 complex, suggesting that this moiety could contain the major RNA-binding site (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The minimal RNA-binding complex of ctPRC2 consists of EBD and BAM domains of EZH2 and the entire EED subunit.
source: In contrast, in the regulatory moiety we identified a minimal RNA-binding complex consisting of EBD and BAM domains of EZH2 and the entire EED subunit, and it had RNA-binding affinity comparable to that of intact core ctPRC2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The minimal RNA-binding complex of ctPRC2 maintains the binding specificity for G-quadruplex RNA.
source: Strikingly, this minimal RNA-binding complex and the regulatory moiety maintained the binding specificity for G-quadruplex RNA (Figure 2C), tested by comparing (GGAA)10 and (GA)20 RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Addition of the EBD and BAM domains to EED increases RNA binding by about 50-fold.
source: The minimal complex consists of EBD and BAM domains of EZH2 and the entire EED subunit, while EED alone binds RNA weakly (Kdapp = 2.7 µM). Addition of the EBD and BAM domains to EED increases the RNA binding by about 50-fold, suggesting that key determinants for RNA binding are located on these two domains of EZH2, with EED providing a platform for their proper 3D architecture.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing binding affinities.

claim: C-terminal truncation of the BAM domain led to a gradual reduction in RNA binding up to 17-fold when the BAM domain was completely deleted.
source: In contrast, C-terminal truncation of the BAM domain (C1-5 mutants) led to a gradual reduction in RNA binding up to 17-fold when the BAM domain was completely deleted.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Four residues (D266, K268, K270 and H272) in the BAM domain of ctPRC2 are important for RNA binding.
source: Thus the better separation-of-function mutant of ctPRC2 is obtained by mutating four residues (D266, K268, K270 and H272) in its BAM domain.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mutant 1 of ctPRC2 caused a three- to fourfold reduction in RNA-binding.
source: We mutated two patches of residues (mutant 1 and 2) in the context of the ternary ctPRC2 complex (EZH2-EED-VEFS of SUZ12) (Figure 3D); mutant 1 caused a three- to fourfold reduction in RNA-binding while mutant 2 had similar binding affinity as the wild type (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Mutant 1 of ctPRC2 had similar methylation activity as the wild type.
source: Mutant 1 had similar methylation activity as the wild type, while mutant 2 suffered greater reduction in catalytic activity (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The 3m hsPRC2 complex shares very similar RNA-binding specificity with the 5m hsPRC2 complex.
source: The 3 m hsPRC2 shared very similar RNA-binding specificity with the 5 m hsPRC2 complex previously characterized (Figure 4A), suggesting that the 3 m complex retains the major RNA-binding sites and could be a suitable model system for studies of PRC2-RNA interaction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The binding affinity for (GGAA)10 RNA was four-fold lower for the 3m relative to the 5m hsPRC2 complex.
source: Interestingly, the binding affinity for (GGAA)10 RNA was four-fold lower for the 3 m relative to the 5 m complex, indicating that additional subunits in the 5 m may enhance the binding to G-quadruplex RNA or stabilize key RNA binding determinants compared to smaller PRC2 3 m complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing the two complexes.

claim: When the N-terminal helix of EZH2 was truncated by 38 residues, binding to (GGAA)10 RNA was dramatically disrupted.
source: When the N-terminal helix was truncated by 38 residues, binding to (GGAA)10 RNA was dramatically disrupted (Figure 4B bottom left, Kdapp > 2 µM), suggesting a potentially important role of this basic helix in RNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The R34A mutant of hsPRC2 exhibited a six- to sevenfold reduction in (GGAA)10 RNA binding.
source: The R34 residue was found to be particularly important in the N-terminal helix (Figure 4B bottom right), because the R34A mutant exhibited a six- to sevenfold reduction in (GGAA)10 RNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HDX-MS identified four regions in hsEZH2 that are perturbed by RNA interaction: 32–42 (Z1), 210–224 (Z2), 512–531 (Z3) and 645–665 (Z4).
source: Comparative deuterium uptake for the RNA bound and apo-EZH2 subunit highlighted four distinctly differentiated regions, 32–42 (Z1), 210–224 (Z2), 512–531 (Z3) and 645–665 (Z4) of human EZH2.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Z1 is located in N-terminal alpha helix of EZH2 preceding EED binding site.
source: Mapping these regions on the crystal structure of ac/hsPRC2 complex results in the following assignments: (1) Z1 is located in N-terminal alpha helix of EZH2 preceding EED binding site
evidence: This is based on mapping HDX-MS data onto crystal structure.

claim: Z2 is located in the disordered region of SANT1.
source: (2) Z2 is located in the disordered region of SANT1
evidence: This is based on mapping HDX-MS data onto crystal structure.

claim: Z3 is located in the disordered linker between SANT2 and cysteine-rich domain of hsEZH2 catalytic and also overlaps the beginning of the first Zn binding motif of EZH2 CXC.
source: (3) Z3 is located in the disordered linker between SANT2 and cysteine-rich domain of hsEZH2 catalytic and also overlaps the beginning of the first Zn binding motif of EZH2 CXC
evidence: This is based on mapping HDX-MS data onto crystal structure.

claim: Z4 maps to i-SET region of EZH2 catalytic domain.
source: (4) Z4 maps to i-SET region of EZH2 catalytic domain (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on mapping HDX-MS data onto crystal structure.

claim: Two regions in EED (290–308 (E1) and 338–350 (E2)) show statistically significant changes in deuterium uptake in the presence of G-quadruplex RNA.
source: While examining EED deuterium uptakes in the presence and absence of G-quadruplex RNA, we noticed two regions 290–308 (E1) and 338–350 (E2) with minor but statistically significant (p-value<0.05) changes in deuterium uptake (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Key residues in human EZH2 important for RNA binding include F32, R34, D36 and K39 in the N-terminal helix, residues 489–494 (PRKKKR) in the CXC domain and K656 in the I-SET helix.
source: In short, we identified several key residues in human EZH2 that are important for RNA binding: F32, R34, D36 and K39 in the N-terminal helix, residues 489–494 (PRKKKR) in the CXC domain and K656 in the I-SET helix of EZH2.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The K39A point mutation of hsPRC2 caused a 5-fold reduction in RNA binding.
source: The K39A point mutation caused a 5-fold reduction in RNA binding, and the triple mutant [F32A D36A K39A] and the quadruple mutant [F32A R34A D36A K39A] led to additional reduction in RNA binding (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The 489–494 NAAIRS substitution mutant of hsPRC2 retained its methyltransferase activity, with a 10-fold reduction in RNA binding.
source: The 489–494 NAAIRS substitution mutant (PRKKKR to NAAIRS) retained its methyltransferase activity, with a 10-fold reduction in RNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The K656A mutant of hsPRC2 bound (GGAA)10 RNA 4–5 fold weaker compared to the wild-type hsPRC2 concurrent with 50% increase of methyltransferase activity.
source: The K656A mutant bound (GGAA)10 RNA 4–5 fold weaker compared to the wild-type hsPRC2 concurrent with 50% increase of methyltransferase activity, while R653A had a modest change in RNA binding and also showed reduced methyltransferase activity, suggesting an important role of K656 in G-quadruplex RNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: When key mutations were combined, the RNA binding defect became more severe, with Kdapp to (GGAA)10 RNA increasing by around 12-fold compared to the wild-type 3m hsPRC2 complex.
source: When we combined the key mutations, the RNA binding defect became more severe, with Kdapp to (GGAA)10 RNA increasing by around 12-fold compared to the wild-type 3 m hsPRC2 complex (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The RNA-binding mutant [F32A R34A D36A K39A and PRKKKR489-494NAAIRS] of 5m hsPRC2 had no defects in assembly compared to the wild-type complex.
source: In addition, when we mutated these residues in the context of the holoenzyme - 5 m hsPRC2 (EZH2-SUZ12-EED-RBBP4-AEBP2), the mutant [F32A R34A D36A K39A and PRKKKR489-494NAAIRS] complex had no defects in assembly compared to the wild-type complex (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The RNA-binding mutant [F32A R34A D36A K39A and PRKKKR489-494NAAIRS] exhibited a significant binding defect to (GGAA)10 RNA.
source: In addition, when we mutated these residues in the context of the holoenzyme - 5 m hsPRC2 (EZH2-SUZ12-EED-RBBP4-AEBP2), the mutant [F32A R34A D36A K39A and PRKKKR489-494NAAIRS] complex had no defects in assembly compared to the wild-type complex (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), but exhibited a significant binding defect to (GGAA)10 RNA in a fluorescent anisotropy binding assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The RNA-binding mutant still showed substantial binding to a GC-rich dsDNA.
source: Importantly, the RNA-binding mutant still showed substantial binding to a GC-rich dsDNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, right panel), providing a clear path for using it as a separation-of-function mutant for future in vivo experiments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Mutating all key residues identified in Z1 and adjacent to Z3 [F32A R34A D36A K39A and PRKKKR489-494NAAIRS] caused a significant reduction in RNA binding in vivo (0.27-fold relative to wild type EZH2, p=0.020).
source: The K39A mutant and [F32A R34A D36A K39A] mutant exhibited moderate defects in interacting with the (GGAA)10 RNA, while mutating all key residues identified in Z1 and adjacent to Z3 [F32A R34A D36A K39A and PRKKKR489-494NAAIRS] caused a significant reduction in RNA binding (0.27-fold relative to wild type EZH2, p=0.020, Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by fRIP experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The RNA-binding specificity of PRC2 is conserved over vast evolutionary distance, from a fungus to human.
source: First, we discovered that the RNA-binding specificity of PRC2 is conserved over vast evolutionary distance, from a fungus to human, which provides new evidence for its functional importance.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing ctPRC2 and hsPRC2.

claim: The majority of RNA-binding residues in PRC2 are located in EZH2.
source: The majority of these residues are located in EZH2, while hsEED also contains two regions - 290–308 (E1) and 338–350 (E2) - that are identified in HDX-MS and potentially important for interacting with RNA.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and HDX-MS data.

claim: The RNA-binding residues in PRC2 are dispersed across the protein surface.
source: The RNA-binding residues are dispersed across the protein surface, which may explain why identifying them by mutagenesis has been so challenging: if any single binding site is affected by mutation, the RNA can still bind to another site(s) and the resultant change in Kdapp is minimal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Almost none of the identified key RNA-binding residues are conserved between ctPRC2 and hsPRC2.
source: Surprisingly, almost none of the identified key RNA-binding residues are conserved between ctPRC2 and hsPRC2, and the domains important for RNA interaction are also different.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the identified residues in both species.

claim: ctPRC2 and hsPRC2 found different paths to achieve the specificity for G-quadruplex RNA, an example of convergent evolution.
source: It is possible that ctPRC2 and hsPRC2 found different paths to achieve the specificity for G-quadruplex RNA, an example of convergent evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Missense mutations of some hsEZH2 residues critical for RNA binding, including R34, K39 and R494, have been identified in cancer patients.
source: Notably, missense mutations of some of the hsEZH2 residues critical for RNA binding, including R34, K39 and R494, have been identified in cancer patients (R34L, K39E and R494S mutations, https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov).
evidence: This is supported by reference to cancer patient database.

claim: RNA binding inhibits PRC2's ability to act as a histone methyltransferase.
source: Given that RNA binding inhibits PRC2's ability to act as a histone methyltransferase, these mutant PRC2 proteins might be expected to have increased activity in vivo, a possibility that remains to be investigated.
evidence: This is based on prior research and speculation about the consequences.

claim: Deletion of residues 342–368 in a purified mouse 4m PRC2 results in no change in binding to a RepA noncoding RNA.
source: [1] deletion of residues 342–368 in a purified mouse 4 m PRC2 (EZH2-EED-SUZ12-RBBP4) results in no change in binding to a RepA noncoding RNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of residues 342–368 in a 3m hsPRC2 complex doesn't affect binding to a (GGAA)10 G-quadruplex RNA.
source: [2] deletion of residues 342–368 in a 3 m hsPRC2 complex (EZH2-EED-VEFS(SUZ12)) doesn't affect binding to a (GGAA)10 G-quadruplex RNA (Figure 4B, middle left)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Deletion of the unstructured region in acEZH2, corresponding to region 342–368 of mEZH2 in the context of the hybrid ac/hsPRC2, does not affect (GGAA)10 RNA binding or the crosslinking to a 24 nt G-quadruplex RNA.
source: [3] deletion of the unstructured region in acEZH2, corresponding to region 342–368 of mEZH2 in the context of the hybrid ac/hsPRC2, does not affect (GGAA)10 RNA binding or the crosslinking to a 24 nt G-quadruplex RNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: RNA and DNA binding by PRC2 are mutually exclusive.
source: Recently, we reported that hsPRC2 also binds to GC-rich dsDNA sequences, and RNA and DNA binding are mutually exclusive (Wang et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: The best-established function of PRC2-RNA interaction is inhibition of PRC2's histone methyltransferase activity.
source: The best-established function of PRC2-RNA interaction at this point is inhibition of PRC2's histone methyltransferase activity (Cifuentes-Rojas et al., 2014; Kaneko et al., 2014; Beltran et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: ctPRC2 was purified as a ternary complex containing EZH2-VEFS peptide and EED peptide.
source: Two polypeptides – an EZH2-VEFS peptide with an N-terminal 2XProtein A tag and a 6XHis tag and an EED peptide with an N-terminal twin-strep tag (IBA Lifesciences) – were expressed in S. cerevisiae strain CB010, and intact ctPRC2 was purified through tandem purification using IgG resin followed by Strep-Tactin resin.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: The regulatory moiety of ctPRC2 contains EED and N-terminal half of EZH2 (ending at SANT1L domain).
source: Regulatory moiety contains EED and N-terminal half of EZH2 (ending at SANT1L domain), and catalytic moiety contains C-terminal half of EZH2 (starting at MCSS domain) fused with VEFS domain of SUZ12.
evidence: This describes the composition of the regulatory moiety based on the experimental design.

claim: The catalytic moiety of ctPRC2 contains C-terminal half of EZH2 (starting at MCSS domain) fused with VEFS domain of SUZ12.
source: Regulatory moiety contains EED and N-terminal half of EZH2 (ending at SANT1L domain), and catalytic moiety contains C-terminal half of EZH2 (starting at MCSS domain) fused with VEFS domain of SUZ12.
evidence: This describes the composition of the catalytic moiety based on the experimental design.

claim: EED alone binds RNA weakly (Kdapp = 2.7 µM).
source: The minimal complex consists of EBD and BAM domains of EZH2 and the entire EED subunit, while EED alone binds RNA weakly (Kdapp = 2.7 µM).
evidence: This is supported by experimental binding data.

claim: When half of EBD was truncated from the N-terminus (N1 mutant), only a twofold reduction in RNA binding was observed.
source: When half of EBD was truncated from the N-terminus (N1 mutant), only a twofold reduction in RNA binding was observed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The VEFS and SANT2L domains of ctPRC2 showed little binding to (GGAA)10 RNA (Kdapp > 5 µM).
source: For the components of the catalytic moiety, the VEFS and SANT2L domains showed little binding to (GGAA)10 RNA (Kdapp > 5 µM), and the CXC-SET domains bound to (GGAA)10 RNA with a 60-fold higher Kdapp compared with wild-type ctPRC2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental binding data.

claim: The CXC-SET domains of ctPRC2 bound to (GGAA)10 RNA with a 60-fold higher Kdapp compared with wild-type ctPRC2.
source: For the components of the catalytic moiety, the VEFS and SANT2L domains showed little binding to (GGAA)10 RNA (Kdapp > 5 µM), and the CXC-SET domains bound to (GGAA)10 RNA with a 60-fold higher Kdapp compared with wild-type ctPRC2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental binding data.

claim: Mutant 2 of ctPRC2 suffered greater reduction in catalytic activity compared to wild type.
source: Mutant 1 had similar methylation activity as the wild type, while mutant 2 suffered greater reduction in catalytic activity (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The amino acid sequence of the BAM domain is not well conserved between ctPRC2 and hsPRC2.
source: The amino acid sequence of the BAM domain is not well conserved between ctPRC2 and hsPRC2, and of the four key RNA-binding residues in the BAM domain of ctPRC2, only D266 is found in hsPRC2.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: Of the four key RNA-binding residues in the BAM domain of ctPRC2, only D266 is found in hsPRC2.
source: The amino acid sequence of the BAM domain is not well conserved between ctPRC2 and hsPRC2, and of the four key RNA-binding residues in the BAM domain of ctPRC2, only D266 is found in hsPRC2.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: Residues 342–368 in an unstructured region of mouse EZH2 were previously reported to be important for RNA interaction.
source: Previously, residues 342–368 (RBD1) in mouse EZH2 were reported to be important for RNA interaction (Kaneko et al., 2010), and this sequence is conserved in hsEZH2.
evidence: This is based on prior published research.

claim: The sequence of residues 342–368 in mouse EZH2 is conserved in hsEZH2.
source: Previously, residues 342–368 (RBD1) in mouse EZH2 were reported to be important for RNA interaction (Kaneko et al., 2010), and this sequence is conserved in hsEZH2.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: A binary complex formed by SUZ12(ΔVEFS) and RBBP4 subunits bound (GGAA)10 RNA very weakly.
source: A binary complex formed by SUZ12(ΔVEFS) and RBBP4 subunits bound (GGAA)10 RNA very weakly (Figure 4B top right), further supporting that the major RNA-binding sites are located in the 3 m complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When the adjacent SANT1 domain was replaced by a (GGS)3GG linker, RNA binding was slightly enhanced.
source: When the adjacent SANT1 domain was replaced by a (GGS)3GG linker, RNA binding was slightly enhanced (Figure 4B middle right), plausibly by reducing the repulsive negative charge in this area or releasing the N-terminal helix to increase its flexibility to accommodate RNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Deuterium uptake was measured at five time points over a period of 480 min for comparison of hsPRC2 against the RNA-hsPRC2 complex.
source: Deuterium uptake was measured at five time points over a period of 480 min for comparison of hsPRC2 against the RNA-hsPRC2 complex.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used for HDX-MS.

claim: HDX-MS provided 91.3%, 96.4%, 99.0% sequence coverage for EZH2, EED, and SUZ12 respectively.
source: A deuterium uptake profile of 258 (EZH2), 149 (EED) and 114 (SUZ12) peptides, generated from inline digest, provided 91.3%, 96.4%, 99.0% sequence coverage for each subunit, respectively.
evidence: This describes the results of the HDX-MS experiment.

claim: EZH2 has highest baseline dynamics amongst the subunits of hsPRC2 3m complex.
source: We first examined the changes in deuterium uptake of the EZH2 subunit, which was previously shown to have highest baseline dynamics amongst the subunits of hsPRC2 3 m complex.
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS data analysis.

claim: Reduction in deuterium uptake for EZH2 in complex with (GGAA)10 RNA suggests that these regions could be on the binding interface with G-quadruplex or impacted in an allosteric fashion.
source: Reduction in deuterium uptake for EZH2 in complex with (GGAA)10 RNA suggests that these regions could be on the binding interface with G-quadruplex or impacted in an allosteric fashion (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HDX-MS data.

claim: Both EED (81-441) and SUZ12-VEFS S583D subunits of 3m hsPRC2 exhibit lower baseline dynamics in the apo-state.
source: Both EED (81-441) and SUZ12-VEFS S583D subunits of 3 m hsPRC2 exhibit lower baseline dynamics in the apo-state.
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS data analysis.

claim: SUZ12-VEFS S1 region is on the interface between SUZ12-VEFS and MCSS domain of EZH2.
source: SUZ12-VEFS S1 region is on the interface between SUZ12-VEFS and MCSS domain of EZH2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on mapping HDX-MS data onto crystal structure.

claim: PRC2 regions with altered deuterium uptake profile could represent the direct G-quadruplex RNA binding interface, or reflect allosteric changes in PRC2 dynamics upon interaction with RNA.
source: PRC2 regions with altered deuterium uptake profile could represent the direct G-quadruplex RNA binding interface, or reflect allosteric changes in PRC2 dynamics upon interaction with RNA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HDX-MS data.

claim: The triple mutant [F32A D36A K39A] and the quadruple mutant [F32A R34A D36A K39A] led to additional reduction in RNA binding compared to K39A alone.
source: The K39A point mutation caused a 5-fold reduction in RNA binding, and the triple mutant [F32A D36A K39A] and the quadruple mutant [F32A R34A D36A K39A] led to additional reduction in RNA binding (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Most RNA-binding mutants of hsPRC2 had no change in catalytic activity.
source: Importantly, H3 methylation activities were tested on all mutants and most had no change in catalytic activity (Figure 6C), except the K656A mutation resulted in an increase in activity (1.5 fold).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The K656A mutation resulted in an increase in methyltransferase activity (1.5 fold).
source: Importantly, H3 methylation activities were tested on all mutants and most had no change in catalytic activity (Figure 6C), except the K656A mutation resulted in an increase in activity (1.5 fold).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Two important separation-of-function mutants were successfully made: the F32A, R34A, D36A and K39A quadruple mutant and the 489–494 NAAIRS substitution mutant.
source: Two important separation-of-function mutants were successfully made (the F32A, R34A, D36A and K39A quadruple mutant and the 489–494 NAAIRS substitution mutant).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The substitution of residues in acEZH2 corresponding to residues 488–510 in hsEZH2 to a glycine-serine linker caused a significant reduction in binding to (GGAA)10 RNA.
source: RNA-binding studies with the chimeric 3 m ac/hsPRC2-3 protein complexes previously used for structural work (Brooun et al., 2016) showed that the substitution of residues in acEZH2 corresponding to residues 488–510 in hsEZH2 to a glycine-serine linker caused a significant reduction in binding to (GGAA)10 RNA, while deletion of the previously reported RNA-binding region (Kaneko et al., 2010) did not affect binding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mutation of the region corresponding to residues 488–510 in ac/hsPRC2 caused loss of crosslinking of the RNA to PRC2.
source: Additionally, an alternative RNA crosslinking approach using a 4-thio-uridine-labeled G-quadruplex RNA supports this region (residues 488–510 adjacent to Z3) as being critical for interaction, because mutation of this region in ac/hsPRC2 caused loss of crosslinking of the RNA to PRC2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The majority of RNA is crosslinked to the EZH2 subunit rather than the other two subunits.
source: This crosslinking experiment also indicated that the majority of RNA is crosslinked to the EZH2 subunit rather than the other two subunits, supporting our conclusion that EZH2 is the most important subunit for RNA interaction.
evidence: This is supported by crosslinking experimental data.

claim: Z4 (645–665) is located at the I-SET alpha-helix that is critical for maintaining catalytically competent PRC2 in basal state via interaction with SAL.
source: Z4 (645–665) is located at the I-SET alpha-helix that is critical for maintaining catalytically competent PRC2 in basal state via interaction with SAL and this region interacts with SRM in the activated PRC2 structure resulting in further increase in catalytic activity.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge and prior research.

claim: R654 in EZH2 is involved in an intramolecular salt bridge and is important for catalysis.
source: (We did not mutate R654 because it is involved in an intramolecular salt bridge and is important for catalysis.)
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge.

claim: R653A mutant had a modest change in RNA binding and also showed reduced methyltransferase activity.
source: The K656A mutant bound (GGAA)10 RNA 4–5 fold weaker compared to the wild-type hsPRC2 concurrent with 50% increase of methyltransferase activity, while R653A had a modest change in RNA binding and also showed reduced methyltransferase activity, suggesting an important role of K656 in G-quadruplex RNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The K39A mutant and [F32A R34A D36A K39A] mutant exhibited moderate defects in interacting with the (GGAA)10 RNA in vivo.
source: The K39A mutant and [F32A R34A D36A K39A] mutant exhibited moderate defects in interacting with the (GGAA)10 RNA, while mutating all key residues identified in Z1 and adjacent to Z3 [F32A R34A D36A K39A and PRKKKR489-494NAAIRS] caused a significant reduction in RNA binding (0.27-fold relative to wild type EZH2, p=0.020, Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by fRIP experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Wild type and mutant EZH2 proteins showed comparable expression levels in HEK293T cells.
source: Three key RNA-binding defected mutants - [K39A], [F32A R34A D36A K39A], and [F32A R34A D36A K39A and PRKKKR489-494NAAIRS] - were expressed in HEK293T cells, and western blots analysis using a FLAG antibody indicated comparable expression levels of the wild type and mutant EZH2 proteins (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Many chromatin-binding proteins do not contain an obvious RNA-binding motif such as an RRM.
source: However, many of these proteins do not contain an obvious RNA-binding motif such as an RRM (RNA recognition motif), and this has hindered critical tests of the function of RNA binding.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of protein structures.

claim: DNMT3 interacts with an RNA at its catalytic domain in a structurally dependent way while two other RNAs can interact at an allosteric site outside the catalytic domain.
source: For example, DNA methyltransferase 3 (DNMT3) has been shown to interact with an RNA at its catalytic domain in a structurally dependent way while two other RNAs can interact at an allosteric site outside the catalytic domain (Holz-Schietinger and Reich, 2012).
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: If any single binding site on PRC2 is affected by mutation, the RNA can still bind to another site(s) and the resultant change in Kdapp is minimal.
source: The RNA-binding residues are dispersed across the protein surface, which may explain why identifying them by mutagenesis has been so challenging: if any single binding site is affected by mutation, the RNA can still bind to another site(s) and the resultant change in Kdapp is minimal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: ctEED contains an extra domain that is adjacent to the N-terminal helix of EZH2.
source: It is interesting that ctEED contains an extra domain that is adjacent to the N-terminal helix of EZH2 (Figure 7), and this extra domain might prevent RNA interaction with the N-terminal helix (Z1 in hsEZH2) due to steric hindrance.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The extra domain in ctEED might prevent RNA interaction with the N-terminal helix (Z1 in hsEZH2) due to steric hindrance.
source: It is interesting that ctEED contains an extra domain that is adjacent to the N-terminal helix of EZH2 (Figure 7), and this extra domain might prevent RNA interaction with the N-terminal helix (Z1 in hsEZH2) due to steric hindrance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural analysis.

claim: R34L and K39E mutations were both identified in lung adenocarcinoma patients.
source: However, it remains unclear what physiological consequences these mutations have in cancer, because each of these heterogeneous mutations was identified in one out of hundreds of patients investigated and in different type of cancers (R34L and K39E were both identified in lung adenocarcinoma patients).
evidence: This is based on cancer patient database information.

claim: Mutant PRC2 proteins with RNA-binding defects might be expected to have increased activity in vivo.
source: Given that RNA binding inhibits PRC2's ability to act as a histone methyltransferase, these mutant PRC2 proteins might be expected to have increased activity in vivo, a possibility that remains to be investigated.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the known function of RNA binding.

claim: In addition to EZH2 overexpression, mutation of RNA-binding residues may also drive PRC2 gain-of-function in cancer.
source: Thus, in addition to EZH2 overexpression, mutation of RNA-binding residues may also drive PRC2 gain-of-function in cancer.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings.

claim: G-quadruplex-forming RNA sequences have been proposed to be largely unfolded in vivo.
source: Recently, G-quadruplex-forming RNA sequences have been proposed to be largely unfolded in vivo (Guo and Bartel, 2016), and it would be interesting to study whether PRC2 can bind and stabilize transiently folded quadruplexes.
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: None of the core PRC2 subunits has an RNA recognition motif (RRM).
source: What elements within PRC2 bind RNA has been unclear, especially since none of the core PRC2 subunits has an RNA recognition motif (RRM).
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of PRC2 subunits.

claim: Three high-resolution crystal structures of the minimal catalytic core of PRC2 have been determined.
source: A 21 Å electron microscopy structure of the human PRC2 complex shed light on its molecular architecture and subunit organization (Ciferri et al., 2012), and recently three high-resolution crystal structures of the minimal catalytic core of PRC2 (EZH2, EED and Suz12-VEFS) were determined.
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: No canonical RNA-binding motif can be identified in the crystal structures of PRC2.
source: Surprisingly, no canonical RNA-binding motif can be identified in these structures.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structures.

claim: The N-terminal helix of EZH2 is bent at Z1 region in a stimulated state of hsPRC2.
source: Evidence of the inter-talk of these regions is that the N-terminal helix of EZH2 is bent at Z1 region in a stimulated state of hsPRC2 indicated in the crystal structure of a H3K27me3-stimulated 3 m hsPRC2 (Justin et al., 2016), bringing in Z2 region to approach the Z1, Z2 and E2 regions to make a more compact RNA binding site.
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis from prior research.

claim: The bending of the N-terminal helix brings Z2 region to approach the Z1, Z2 and E2 regions to make a more compact RNA binding site.
source: Evidence of the inter-talk of these regions is that the N-terminal helix of EZH2 is bent at Z1 region in a stimulated state of hsPRC2 indicated in the crystal structure of a H3K27me3-stimulated 3 m hsPRC2 (Justin et al., 2016), bringing in Z2 region to approach the Z1, Z2 and E2 regions to make a more compact RNA binding site.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural analysis.

claim: EED-E2 region is adjacent to Z1 site on the EZH2 subunit.
source: Mapping of E2 (EED) region on the crystal structure of 3 m ac/hs PRC2 places it adjacent to Z1 site on the EZH2 subunit, suggesting that it could be part of putative G-quadruplex binding interface formed by EZH2-Z1, Z2 and EED-E2 regions (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on mapping HDX-MS data onto crystal structure.

claim: EED-E2 could be part of putative G-quadruplex binding interface formed by EZH2-Z1, Z2 and EED-E2 regions.
source: Mapping of E2 (EED) region on the crystal structure of 3 m ac/hs PRC2 places it adjacent to Z1 site on the EZH2 subunit, suggesting that it could be part of putative G-quadruplex binding interface formed by EZH2-Z1, Z2 and EED-E2 regions (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on HDX-MS and structural data.
